summary.value:
This paper introduces a new "Structure-to-text" method for LLMs. Such methods usually employ simple ways to serialize the structure to allow the LLM to encode it. A typical example is linearizing a Direct Acyclic Graph into a as string that can be tokenized. This approaches however loose important structure information. The proposal here is to 

1. enrich the conventional encoding with additional position embeddings reflecting the graph structructure. 
2. obtain these from a modified Laplacian of the graph. Concretely they use the "Magnetic Laplacian" which leverages a complex valued representation to capture graph directionality

The usefulness of the method is show in Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR)-to-text. This is a well known meaning representation expresses as directed acyclic graphs with both labeled edges and nodes.

strengths.value:
1. The idea is clear and addresses an interesting problem. Intuitively there has to be a better way of encoding graph information than simple linearization

2. The method proposed, based on the "Magnetic Laplacian" encoding of graphs is novel in its application to Structure-to-text (to the best of my knowledge) although it has been used for Graph Neural Networks and other purposes in the past. 

3. The method also does not require additional models and seem relatively simple in terms of network modifications

weaknesses.value:
My main criticism is about relevance. 

1. The area of structure-to-text seems to be fading a bit since it is clear that large LLMs can perform this task relatively well. It is best to avoid closed-source LLMs but a baseline using some well known SoTa LLM is a useful reference. LLMs larger than 3B would also be in order here. The suspicion is that, as models grow larger, the advantage of encoding will also reduce.
 
2. and more clearly Abstract Meaning Representation, and other liguistic representations seem to be not relevant any more for representing information. At least other usual Structure-to-text datasets like WebNLG and similar could enrich the paper further. I don't know if there is any more recent dataset on this area, if not, this further substantiates my point (1)

Aside from this the experimental setup could be improved. Only the LLaMa models show clear gains, and even in this case it is not clear whats if there is statistical relevance. Since the metrics used are bounded between 0 and 1 standard deviation is not ideal, but given that many numbers are close to 0.5 it may help at least get an idea. Another option is to run a boostrap paired test which would work for such metrics.

questions.value: What is the standard deviation in the results shown? knowing this or the statistical significance would be great

comment.value:
Thank you for the thoughtful review. We appreciate the positive feedback on the novelty and simplicity of our approach for structure-to-text generation in LLMs. We address your points below.

### Value of structural encoding relative to model scale (W1)
**Comment**: The area of structure-to-text seems to be fading a bit since it is clear that large LLMs can perform this task relatively well. It is best to avoid closed-source LLMs but a baseline using some well known SoTa LLM is a useful reference. LLMs larger than 3B would also be in order here. The suspicion is that, as models grow larger, the advantage of encoding will also reduce.

**Response**: We clarify current limitations of SoTA LLMs on the task of structure-to-text generation, and the value of explicitly encoding structural information with the following three observations.

(1) **Fine-tuning remains essential, even for large LLMs.**
Table 2 shows that GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini, despite being far larger and trained on much broader corpora, perform substantially worse in zero-shot and few-shot settings than a 3B open-source model fine-tuned on AMR. This suggests that, in our specific prompting setup, structure-to-text generation remains difficult for large general-purpose models without task-specific fine-tuning, and that increased scale alone does not compensate for the structural demands of AMRs.
(2) **SAFT becomes more valuable as structural complexity increases.**
Our stratified analysis (Figures 2 and 3) shows that for every model family, SAFT's improvement over standard fine-tuning grows with graph depth and document complexity. Even the larger backbones (e.g., LLaMA 3B, Qwen 3B) show minimal differences on simple AMRs but increasing gains as graphs become more complex. This suggests that explicitly encoding structure remains useful, regardless of model size, and is most beneficial when structural complexity increases.

(3) **We do not observe a trend where larger models rely less on structure.**
The model-scale analysis we introduce in Appendix C.2 and Figure 8 shows no monotonic relationship between model size and SAFT's gains over FT. Some families benefit more at smaller scales, others at larger ones. We do not identify the pattern "more parameters → less need for structure". Our results do not support a systematically diminishing-gains trend with size.

Taken together, **these results do not support the hypothesis that structural encoding becomes unnecessary as models grow larger**. Instead, they indicate that (i) fine-tuning is required even for the strongest LLMs, (ii) explicit structure helps most when complexity increases, and (iii) SAFT provides benefits across the tested scales, and we do not observe a diminishing-returns trend within this range.

### Relevance and scope of structured inputs (W2)

**Comment:** Abstract Meaning Representation, and other liguistic representations seem to be not relevant any more for representing information. [...] Other usual Structure-to-text datasets like WebNLG and similar could enrich the paper further.

**Response:** Recent work indicates that AMR and related semantic graph formalisms remain in active use, especially in applications where explicit meaning structure, interpretability, and control over semantic content are important [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] . There is also empirical evidence that current LLMs can face limitations on tasks that require deeper semantic or relational understanding when they are guided only by surface prompts [6, 7, 8]. Our own results reinforce this: as shown in Table 2, even very large instruction-tuned models, such as GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini, perform far below a 3B model fine-tuned with SAFT, which suggests that strong pre-trained LLMs do not automatically recover the underlying structure of linearized AMRs.
We agree that applying SAFT to additional graph-to-text datasets would broaden the empirical scope. In this submission, however, we explicitly focus on AMR 3.0 and DocAMR because they include rich semantic phenomena such as reentrancies, non-tree structure, and document-level coreference. These properties make them a challenging setting for assessing whether a model can make systematic use of graph structure rather than relying only on the input's linearized form. Other structure-to-text datasets, such as the suggested WebNLG, are valuable but typically contain smaller and more regular structures that resemble sets of RDF triples or shallow trees. They are useful benchmarks, but they place less emphasis on the kinds of structural challenges that are central to this work.
We clarify in the paper that while SAFT is conceptually general, this manuscript's goal is to show SAFT capabilities to improve over conventional FT, especially at increasing structure complexities. We view the extension of SAFT to other structure-to-text datasets as an interesting direction, which would however require specific graph transformations and an adaptation of the graph positional embeddings.

### Bootstrap paired test (W3 and Q1)
**Comment**: Since the metrics used are bounded between 0 and 1 standard deviation is not ideal, but given that many numbers are close to 0.5 it may help at least get an idea. Another option is to run a boostrap paired test which would work for such metrics.

**Response**: In the revised manuscript we have added a **bootstrap paired significance test** to evaluate whether SAFT's improvements over standard fine-tuning (FT) are reliable under resampling. For each model, we generate 50 bootstrap replicates by resampling the evaluation set with replacement and compare SAFT and FT on each replicate.
Across almost all models and metrics, SAFT wins on the large majority of bootstrap samples. This is visible in the **win-rate matrix** now included in Appendix C.3 (Figure 9), which shows that SAFT outperforms FT on the large majority of bootstrap samples across models and metrics.
To complement this, we report **bootstrap mean ± standard deviation** for BLEU, and ChrF (Table 6). We report the table here for completeness: 

| Model           | Variant   | BLEU         | ChrF         |
|:----------------|:----------|:-------------|:-------------|
| Gemma (2B)      | FT        | 52.97 ± 0.49 | 69.74 ± 0.29 |
|                 | SAFT      | 53.01 ± 0.48 | 69.98 ± 0.30 |
| LLaMA 3.2 (1B)  | FT        | 45.64 ± 0.55 | 65.74 ± 0.37 |
|                 | SAFT      | **47.75 ± 0.54** | **67.65 ± 0.33** |
| LLaMA 3.2 (3B)  | FT        | 53.52 ± 0.40 | 71.70 ± 0.25 |
|                 | SAFT      | 54.45 ± 0.44 | 72.40 ± 0.30 |
| Qwen 2.5 (0.5B) | FT        | 42.68 ± 0.40 | 63.14 ± 0.30 |
|                 | SAFT      | 42.94 ± 0.52 | 62.94 ± 0.30 |
| Qwen 2.5 (1.5B) | FT        | 50.66 ± 0.46 | 68.69 ± 0.30 |
|                 | SAFT      | 51.69 ± 0.54 | **70.70 ± 0.34** |
| Qwen 2.5 (3B)   | FT        | 51.75 ± 0.50 | 69.33 ± 0.37 |
|                 | SAFT      | 52.00 ± 0.45 | **70.44 ± 0.29** |

For some models the improvements are small, and the bootstrap distribution reflects this. Overall, the bootstrap analysis supports the consistency of SAFT's gains while remaining agnostic about cases where the SAFT-FT gap is smaller.

### Final comment
Thank you again for your valuable feedback and suggestions. We welcome further comments that you believe would improve the paper.

### References

[1]: A Survey of AMR Applications (https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.390) 

[2]: Survey of Abstract Meaning Representation: Then, Now, Future (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03229)

[3]: Don't Forget to Connect! Improving RAG with Graph-based Reranking (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.18414)

[4]: Large Language Models Meet Text-Attributed Graphs: A Survey of Integration Frameworks and Applications (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21131)

[5]: Structured Information Matters: Incorporating Abstract Meaning Representation into LLMs for Improved Open-Domain Dialogue Evaluation (https://openreview.net/forum?id=9GkTadOcvH)

[6]: A Survey on Large Language Model Reasoning Failures (https://openreview.net/forum?id=hsgMn4KBFG)

[7]: Potential and Limitations of LLMs in Capturing Structured Semantics: A Case Study on SRL (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06410v1)

[8]: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity (https://openreview.net/forum?id=YghiOusmvw)

summary.value: The paper focuses on the problem of generating natural language sentences or documents from abstract meaning representation (AMR) graphs.  The baseline approach is to finetune a language model (1B-3B parameter range) specifically for this task; for Qwen/Llama/Gemma models this already outperforms published systems.   An AMR graph is first converted into a semantics-preserving graph (SPG).   The innovation in this paper is to introduce a new kind of positional embedding specific for AMR, derived from the (magnetic) Laplacian of the AMR graph.  The positional embedding is concatenated with intra-node token positional embeddings, before applying to standard LM embedding. By combining this positional embedding scheme with standard fine-tuning method (using LoRA), the authors arrive at what they call “Structure-Aware Fine-Tuning.”   The motivation is that doing so will help the model “to better capture graph topology and long-range dependencies.”  Experimental results show consistent improvements across base models and evaluation metrics on the AMR-to-text task, compared to the more conventional finetuning approach.  Additional experiments show that improvements hold up when evaluating on a harder document-level task and that improvements are greater on “deeper” (and supposedly more challenging) AMR graph inputs.

strengths.value:
The paper is generally clearly presented and well motivated.  The magnetic Laplacian idea is elegant, and this reviewer learned something new from the paper.  The method is easy-to-follow and uses graph theory tools like magnetic Laplacian. The math formulae in the paper are helpful.  (Though the reviewer did need to spend a few minutes chatting with a language model to get some intuition about the magnetic Laplacian; the paper could do more to help readers here.)

The experimental results are good, and even better when one looks at the appendix.  I especially appreciate inclusion of the document-length experiments.  I also appreciate the complexity-stratified results. They give strong evidence that the approach is good at handling complex AMRs. 

Experiments compare with previous strong approaches and standard fine-tuning methods on standard AMR 3.0 benchmark.

The paper included comprehensive details in the appendix, including implementation, dataset and related works. Readers who are not familiar with this field should be able to understand the paper.

weaknesses.value:
There is no discussion of the computational cost of the approach in the main paper, either in absolute terms (complexity of calculating the position embeddings – though this is in the appendix, increase in input token count, etc.) or relative to the baseline (at finetuning time, at inference time – this comparison is not even in the appendix).  Readers will want to know what they have to pay to get the quality improvements, both up front to finetune and at inference time.  I think some of this discussion should be in the main paper.

There are key details missing about the finetuning.  How many epochs (this is only in the appendix)?  Is the loss the negative log probability of the outputs conditioned on the input graphs?  (This seems like the only choice, but it’s not stated.)  Or something else?  Which parameters are updated?  One supposes  LoRA parameters and the new ones that transform the graph representation for input as tokens (f_theta), but it’s not stated clearly.

I wasn’t entirely clear about what motivated the desire to avoid architectural changes.  I suspect it has to do with preserving the LM’s existing abilities.  But then there are no experiments to measure how much the finetuning for AMR-to-text degrades the models’ other capabilities.

It seems like a big part of what is learned during finetuning is getting the new positional embeddings to “mesh” with the existing ones.  But the positional embeddings in the base models are not discussed at all.  Are they all sinusoidal?  Should some elements of the graph embeddings be designed around the positional embeddings of the base model?  Given that the technical novelty of the paper hinges on these new embeddings, there’s a missed opportunity to explore what happens during learning.

The claim in the abstract/introduction about general applicability for structured inputs is, I think, a bit overstated.  At the very least, some discussion of how this paper’s specific technical idea could apply to other settings beyond the labeled DAGs of AMR seems necessary to justify that argument.  Even better would be experiments.

The baselines seem well chosen, but this reviewer wondered why the comparison to proprietary, un-finetune-able models was buried in the appendix.  The fact that stronger/larger LMs perform poorly on this task seems to strengthen the paper a lot.  I would suggest adding few-shot experiments there, as well, and maybe testing a few more “frontier” models.

All experiments are conducted with LoRA, which limits the extent to which the model can be adapted or fine-tuned. Even though LoRA has been shown powerful enough on many natural language tasks, it is not discussed if it’s sufficient to do LoRA for AMR-to-text tasks. AMR data is relatively rare in the pre-training corpus of LLMs, so maybe full-finetuning would show larger improvements on this task. Will SAFT improve the performance under the full-finetuning setting? It’s possible that SAFT improvement will be marginal and only works for parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings. If the computation resources are limited, I recommend doing experiments with increasing LoRA rank to approximate the trend. However, full-finetune experiments would be the best.


In Table 1, all previous baselines are worse than most of the FT settings. This is perhaps due to the weak backbone of the baselines — BiBL and SPRING are based on BART, StructAdapt is based on T5. So, the results of FT and SAFT in Table 1 are not fully comparable with the previous baselines. All of these LLMs like LLaMA, Qwen, and Gemma are pretrained on a lot of “extra” data.  This raises the question of whether the positional encoding scheme is really the reason the approach is “state of the art”.
 
Some qualitative error analysis would be helpful.

Minor points, easy to fix:

Bold-italic U is introduced just before equation 2 with no definition or connection to earlier objects.

Equation 10 and bold-italic X is unnecessary, as it is never reused.

Table 1:  what are the parenthesized percentages in the table?

I think the DocAMR setting is not “zero-shot”. DocAMR is still on the same task and it’s built from AMR 3.0. 

In table 10, please include the size of DocAMR.

questions.value:
In Table 1, I see a trend that the improvements on larger models are smaller. Does it suggest that SAFT only works for small models? Since the margins of most improvement are small ( < 2% absolute), it’s better to report average performance over different random seeds for both methods.

Figure 2(a) shows almost zero gap for Qwen when z is small. Any explanation for this phenomenon?

Can we use different prompts to fine-tune LLMs to understand AMR graphs so that users can talk with LLMs directly about the AMR graph? This will enable a wider use of the positional embedding.

In section 3.3, a pretrained LLM decoder is decomposed into DECODE and EMBED. Does EMBED include the LLM’s original positional embedding? If not, then the position of the AMR in the prompt is not encoded. According to the prompt in B.3.1, the position of “L_A” matters. However, if EMBED includes the LLM’s original positional embedding, that imposes a sequential order onto “T_L” and thus different node numberings give different final embeddings. Please clarify this.

The test set of AMR 3.0 only has 1898 samples. It is sufficient for general tests, but could be too few for stratified analysis. How many examples do we have for z>=8? It would be better to plot the distribution of z on the test set of AMR 3.0. Similarly, it would be better to have the plot for DocAMR, which I believe would be even sparser when z ranges from 0 to 35.

What kind of LLMs are fine-tuned for the AMR-to-text task? Base models or post-trained models? Please include the specific tags of the models. According to the prompt in B.3.1, they might be the base models since there is an ending token encouraging completion. However, GPT-4o-mini is a chat model, so the prompt should be redesigned and optimized for experiments in C.4. Please enclose the prompt for GPT-4o-mini. It should contain necessary content for adapting the task to natural language and also include common techniques like CoT. GPT-4o might outperform SAFT but that’s acceptable since they are much larger and pre-trained on more data.

DocAMR is built from part of AMR 3.0. Does it include the training split of AMR 3.0? If so, there will be data leakage and the evaluation is no longer meaningful. According to the DocAMR paper, only 9 test graphs are not coming from the training split of AMR 3.0, which are too few.

comment.value:
We thank you for your constructive and thorough review, and appreciate your comments on the clarity of presentation and on the extent of our evaluations. We answer your questions and concerns below.

### Computational cost and runtime (W1)
**Comment**: There is no discussion of the computational cost of the approach in the main paper, either in absolute terms (complexity of calculating the position embeddings – though this is in the appendix, increase in input token count, etc.) or relative to the baseline (at fine-tuning time, at inference time – this comparison is not even in the appendix). Readers will want to know what they have to pay to get the quality improvements, both up front to fine-tune and at inference time. I think some of this discussion should be in the main paper.

**Response**: As correctly mentioned, the full complexity and runtime measurements are already reported in **Appendix C.5** and **Tables 9 and 10**. Since space in the main paper is limited, we added a short pointer in Section 4 to direct readers to this analysis.
We would like to clarify that, compared to FT, SAFT's only additional costs are (i) the computation of graph positional encodings, and (ii) the training of a simple 2-layer MLP to project them in the latent space of the LLM. FLOPs during the transformer forward pass, token length, and hidden dimensionality remain unchanged relative to standard FT.
- Regarding (i): as reported in Table 10, this preprocessing adds 0.01 seconds on AMR 3.0 and 0.28 seconds on DocAMR on average, which is small relative to overall inference time.
- Regarding (ii): the MLP has two layers mapping respectively from $\mathbb{R}^{2k+d} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_\textrm{emb}}$ and $\mathbb{R}^{d_\textrm{emb}} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_\textrm{emb}}$, hence adding $d_\textrm{emb}(2k+d + d_\textrm{emb} + 2) \approx d_\textrm{emb}^2$ additional parameters, which is negligible compared to the LLM's parameter count.

Taken together, this means that SAFT introduces only a very small overhead on top of standard fine-tuning, while typically improving performance in our experiments. We therefore see SAFT not as a heavier alternative, but as a practical modification of standard fine-tuning when structured graph inputs are available.
We have added a clarifying sentence in Appendix C.5.

### Discussion on experimental setup (W2)
**Comment**: How many epochs (this is only in the appendix)? Is the loss the negative log probability of the outputs conditioned on the input graphs? (This seems like the only choice, but it's not stated.) Or something else? Which parameters are updated? One supposes LoRA parameters and the new ones that transform the graph representation for input as tokens (f_theta), but it's not stated clearly.

**Response**: The experimental setup is summarized in **Section 4.1**, with full hyperparameter configurations, including the number of epochs, provided in **Appendix B.3.1**. 
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the missing specification about the training loss we use and the parameters we train/fine-tune. We use the standard **cross-entropy loss for autoregressive decoding**. During fine-tuning, we optimize the LoRA parameters of the backbone model as well as the parameters of the lightweight MLP projection $f_\theta$ that maps the graph positional encodings into the embedding space. We have added a short clarification in **Appendix B.3**.

### Motivation for avoiding architectural changes (W3)
**Comment**: I wasn't entirely clear about what motivated the desire to avoid architectural changes. I suspect it has to do with preserving the LM's existing abilities. 

**Response**: Our motivation for avoiding architectural changes is practical rather than aimed at preserving general-purpose abilities. We sought a method that can be applied directly to existing pre-trained LLMs without modifying their attention or feedforward blocks, as such modifications typically require custom and non-trivial implementations or adaptations. By introducing structure-aware information only through the embedding layer, SAFT remains compatible with standard decoder-only architectures, model-agnostic, and avoids adding computation within the Transformer stack.

### Positional encodings and their interaction with SAFT (W4.1)
**Comment**: The positional embeddings in the base models are not discussed. Are they sinusoidal? Should some elements of the graph embeddings be designed around the positional embeddings of the base model? 

**Response**: We do not modify the positional encoding mechanism of the underlying LLMs. The native positional encodings used by each model remain active during both fine-tuning and inference. In our experiments, all backbones are recent decoder-only architectures that utilize rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) within the attention blocks, rather than sinusoidal embeddings. 
SAFT operates only at the input embedding level by adding AMR-specific positional encodings before the Transformer layers. This means that structural and sequential information are injected through two separate and complementary channels: RoPE continues to provide token-level positional information within the attention mechanism, while SAFT supplies graph-structural information through the embeddings. We intentionally do not co-design SAFT with a specific positional encoding scheme, as this keeps the method architecture-agnostic and directly applicable to different pretrained LLMs without modification. We clarified this in the revised manuscript (lines 275–277, and footnote 2, page 6).

### Embedding analysis (W4.2)
**Comment**: Given that the technical novelty of the paper hinges on these new embeddings, there's a missed opportunity to explore what happens during learning.

**Response**: Thank you for the insightful comment. We have added a geometric analysis on the effects of adding AmrPE to the text token embeddings X in **Section 4.6** and **Figure 4**, which shows that the proposed AmrPEs are largely orthogonal to the semantic embedding space, expanding the representational subspace rather than overwriting it. In particular, we highlight that:
1. AmrPEs have a similar order of magnitude to X, ensuring that they are not obscured by X nor do they obscure X during training; 
2. The directions of our AmrPEs (structural-level semantics) are approximately orthogonal to the directions of X (textual-level semantics), demonstrating that AmrPEs add structure-level information in different directions than the textual-level semantics; 
3. When projected into the 2D PCA of X, AmrPEs express the most variance across one main direction (PC2), while the remaining variance is spread across a few more directions.
4. As a consequence of point (3), AmrPEs introduce a coherent and consistent directional shift along a few dimensions in the latent space, effectively "moving" textual representation to a different subspace;
5. The combined representations (H = X + AmrPE) span a higher-level dimensional space than X, indicating that structural information expands representational capacity, rather than collapsing it.

We believe these are very interesting insights that strengthen our contribution and motivate future work in this direction.

### Impact on general abilities (W5.1)
**Comment**: There are no experiments to measure how much the finetuning for AMR-to-text degrades the models' other capabilities.

**Response**: This work aims to improve AMR-to-text generation, and we do not claim preservation of broad language abilities, which is why the original submission did not include general-purpose capability evaluations. The geometric analysis we discussed above (and in Section 4.6) also helps address the present concern. As shown in Figure 4, the structural information introduced by SAFT appears as an additional component in the token representations that is largely separate from the semantic patterns learned during pretraining. Intuitively, adding a component that encodes graph structure without displacing the existing semantic dimensions may reduce interference with the usual token semantics that support general abilities. While this is not a direct test of broad capabilities, it clarifies how SAFT incorporates structure. We updated the text (end of section 4.6) to include this consideration.

comment.value:
### Generalization to other domains (W5.2)
**Comment**: Some discussion of how this paper's specific technical idea could apply to other settings beyond the labeled DAGs of AMR seems necessary to justify that argument. Even better would be experiments.

**Response**: As explicitly mentioned in the title and throughout the paper, we propose a conceptually general framework for encoding graph information during LLM fine-tuning; however, our evaluation focuses on AMR-to-text generation. Since SAFT operates entirely at the input-embedding level and relies only on having a graph-structured input aligned with text tokens, it is conceptually applicable to other settings such as semantic role graphs or discourse-level graphs.
We agree that extending the method to additional domains would be valuable, although it is beyond the scope of this submission. To clarify how SAFT could be adapted more broadly, we added a short discussion in **Appendix C.6** outlining the requirements for applying the method to other graph-text tasks, and we revised Lines 78–79 to distinguish clearly between conceptual applicability and empirical claims.

### Visibility of large-model baselines and prompting (W6)
**Comment**: The baselines seem well chosen, but this reviewer wondered why the comparison to proprietary, un-finetune-able models was buried in the appendix. The fact that stronger/larger LMs perform poorly on this task seems to strengthen the paper a lot. I would suggest adding few-shot experiments there, as well, and maybe testing a few more “frontier” models.

**Response**: We appreciate your recognition of the strength of those findings. In line with this suggestion, we moved the results for larger proprietary models into the main evaluation (**Table 2, Section 4.5**). The table now includes both zero-shot and few-shot prompting results for GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o. These additions make the contrast clearer: even very strong models under prompting lag behind much smaller FT and SAFT models. We believe this strengthens the overall narrative by highlighting the importance of fine-tuning and, even more, the explicit encoding of structural information for AMR-to-text generation.

### Scaling LoRA vs. full fine-tuning (W7)
**Comment**: Will SAFT improve the performance under the full-finetuning setting? It's possible that SAFT improvement will be marginal and only works for parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings. If the computation resources are limited, I recommend doing experiments with increasing LoRA rank to approximate the trend. However, full-finetune experiments would be the best.

**Response**: Our experiments focus on parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) because AMR supervision is limited, and we evaluate several different pretrained LLMs, making full-model fine-tuning impractical in this setting.
To probe scaling behavior within this regime, we already evaluate multiple LoRA ranks (for example, LLaMA 3.2B at ranks 8 and 32, and Qwen2.5 0.5B at ranks 16 and 32; see Tables 4–5 in Appendix B.3.1). Across these settings, standard fine-tuning shows diminishing or unstable gains as rank increases, whereas SAFT remains robust and often continues to improve. While we can't provide a full evaluation at different LoRA ranks at present (due to the expensive fine-tuning and hyperparameter tuning process), we view a systematic study of those settings as valuable future work, but beyond the practical scope of the current work.

### Backbone strength vs. structure-aware FT contribution (W8)
**Comment**: In Table 1, all previous baselines are worse than most of the FT settings. This is perhaps due to the weak backbone of the baselines — BiBL and SPRING are based on BART, StructAdapt is based on T5. So, the results of FT and SAFT in Table 1 are not fully comparable with the previous baselines. All of these LLMs like LLaMA, Qwen, and Gemma are pretrained on a lot of “extra” data. This raises the question of whether the positional encoding scheme is really the reason the approach is “state of the art”.

**Response**: Differences in backbone strength do affect absolute performance, and the pretrained LLMs we use are indeed stronger than the BART- and T5-based architectures underlying prior AMR systems. For this reason, our core methodological evaluation does not solely rely on cross-architecture comparisons. Instead, we isolate the contribution of SAFT by comparing it directly to standard fine-tuning across Qwen, LLaMA, and Gemma families. These controlled comparisons show a consistent pattern:
1. Large instruction-tuned models used in zero-shot or few-shot settings perform below specialized AMR systems, so model scale alone does not address AMR's structural requirements (Table 2);
2. Fine-tuned LLMs (FT) yield substantial gains over specialized AMR systems;
3. SAFT provides further improvements over FT across all architectures.

Overall, this suggests that the gains attributed to SAFT cannot be attributed solely to the model's size. The method adds value beyond fine-tuning by incorporating AMR structure into the model's representations, and our state-of-the-art result reflects this combination.


### Qualitative behavior and error analysis (W9)
**Comment**: Some qualitative error analysis would be helpful.

**Response**: We have expanded the appendix to include representative outputs from both the fine-tuned baseline (FT) and our SAFT model on LLaMA 3B (**Appendix G**). These examples are selected in a principled manner using smoothed sentence-level BLEU distributions and relative performance percentiles to avoid cherry-picking. For each category (cases where SAFT is substantially better, where FT is better, where both models perform well, and where both perform poorly) we present five instances along with their reference sentences, together with detailed diff highlighting. This allows readers to inspect specific lexical, structural, and semantic divergences that characterize each failure mode.

### Effect of model scale (Q1.1)
**Comment**: In Table 1, I see a trend that the improvements on larger models are smaller. Does it suggest that SAFT only works for small models? 

**Response**: After carefully examining Table 1, **we do not find a consistent pattern in which larger models receive smaller gains from SAFT compared to FT**. We report here a table sorted by model size:

| Model     | Size (B) | BLEU gain (abs)  | BLEU gain (rel) | ChrF gain (abs) | ChrF gain (rel) |
| --------- | -------- | ---------------- | --------------- | --------------- | --------------- |
| Qwen      | 0.5      | +0.2             | +0.5%           | +0.3            | +0.4%           |
| LLaMA     | 1.0      | +2.3             | +5.1%           | +1.0            | +1.4%           |
| Qwen      | 1.5      | +1.2             | +2.4%           | +0.8            | +1.1%           |
| Gemma     | 2.0      | +0.04            | +0.1%           | +0.1            | +0.1%           |
| Qwen      | 3.0      | +0.3             | +0.6%           | +2.7            | +3.7%           |
| LLaMA     | 3.0      | +0.7             | +1.3%           | +0.5            | +0.7%           |

As shown in the reordered table, the relative improvements fluctuate across model sizes in a non-monotonic way, and the two metrics disagree on where the highest gains occur. For example, the 1B LLaMA model shows the strongest relative BLEU improvement, whereas the 3B Qwen model exhibits the strongest relative ChrF improvement. Conversely, the 2B Gemma model shows the smallest gains on both metrics. **This inconsistency makes it difficult to support a simple interpretation in which SAFT primarily benefits smaller models**. Instead, the gains appear to depend on the interaction between architecture, model family, and size, rather than size alone.
To clarify this, we have added a dedicated subsection in **Appendix C.2**, where we visualize the relative BLEU and ChrF gains as a function of model size. The resulting scatter plots (**Figure 8**) indicate that neither metric exhibits a monotonic scaling trend, and even within individual families, the direction of change varies. This reinforces our conclusion that SAFT does not preferentially benefit small models and that model scale alone might not be a reliable predictor of SAFT's improvement.

### On variability and multiple seeds (Q1.2)
**Comment**: Since the margins of most improvement are small ( < 2% absolute), it's better to report average performance over different random seeds for both methods.

**Response**: We agree that multi-seed evaluation would indeed provide stronger statistical guarantees. However, multi-seed fine-tuning across six LLM backbones, multiple LoRA ranks, and hyperparameters is computationally prohibitive in our cluster setting. To provide principled statistical evidence without retraining all models, we incorporated two complementary analyses in the revised manuscript (**Appendix C.3**).

1. We report **bootstrap mean ± standard deviation** for BLEU, and ChrF (Table 6). Standard deviations are small (typically ±0.3–0.5 BLEU), indicating that the observed FT/SAFT differences are not artifacts of sampling noise.
2. We include a **paired bootstrap win-rate analysis** (Figure 9). For each model and metric, we compute the fraction of bootstrap resamples in which SAFT outperforms FT. SAFT achieves high win rates across most models, including 100% wins for both LLaMA variants on BLEU and ChrF, as well as consistently strong wins for Qwen 1.5B and Qwen 3B. Even in cases where the mean improvement is small, the win-rate analysis indicates that SAFT outperforms FT in the majority of bootstrap replicates. 

Together, these results demonstrate a clear and stable pattern: **SAFT typically improves over FT, with gains ranging from marginal to substantial depending on model and metric**. Running full multi-seed training would further quantify across-run variance, but this lies beyond our practical computing budget.

### Interpretation of near-zero gap at low complexity (Q2)
**Question**: Figure 2(a) shows almost zero gap for Qwen when z is small. Any explanation for this phenomenon?

**Response**: The near-zero gap for Qwen (and for Gemma 2B) in the lowest structural-complexity bins aligns with our interpretation of where SAFT provides value. When AMRs are very simple and the alignment between nodes and tokens is direct, standard fine-tuning already captures the required local relationships, so adding structural encodings yields little additional benefit. As structural complexity increases, the task requires modeling longer-range and more intertwined dependencies, and in these regions, SAFT reliably widens the gap over FT, as shown in Figures 2 and 3.

### Conversational access to AMR structure (Q3)
**Comment**: Can we use different prompts to fine-tune LLMs to understand AMR graphs so that users can talk with LLMs directly about the AMR graph? This will enable a wider use of the positional embedding.

**Response**: This is an exciting suggestion and aligns well with a broader vision of AMR-aware language models [1]. SAFT integrates AMR structure into token representations, but in our current setup, the model learns to use this information only to generate text from the input AMR. It is not trained to reference, inspect, or reason explicitly about nodes, edges, or subgraphs in a conversational setting.
Supporting direct interaction with AMR content would require additional supervision and objectives designed for graph querying or explanation, as well as corresponding evaluation protocols. We see this as a natural extension of SAFT's representational strengths and a promising direction for future work.

### Clarification on the role of EMBED and positional information (Q4)
**Comment**: In section 3.3, a pretrained LLM decoder is decomposed into DECODE and EMBED. Does EMBED include the LLM's original positional embedding? If not, then the position of the AMR in the prompt is not encoded. According to the prompt in B.3.1, the position of “L_A” matters. However, if EMBED includes the LLM's original positional embedding, that imposes a sequential order onto “T_L” and thus different node numberings give different final embeddings. Please clarify this.

**Response:** In our implementation, EMBED contains only the pretrained token embedding matrix of the decoder-only LLM. It does not include the model's positional encoding. After tokens are embedded, SAFT's structural vector is added, and the combined representation is then passed into the Transformer stack (DECODE). The model's native positional mechanism (RoPE) is applied inside DECODE, exactly as in standard fine-tuning.
The AMR positional encodings introduced by SAFT are therefore an independent, structure-aware signal that does not alter or replace the LLM's own positional encoding. The alignment function $\sigma_A$ maps each AMR node to its corresponding token span, so the structural vector is attached to the correct content tokens regardless of traversal order or node numbering in the linearization. Before RoPE is applied, SAFT's contribution is thus insensitive to the serialization order and depends only on the graph's topology.
RoPE still introduces positional information during attention, but this is identical to what happens in standard fine-tuning. SAFT's role is to add graph-aware information alongside the textual signal, not to enforce invariance to sequence order. 

### DocAMR test set (Q7)
**Comment**: DocAMR is built from part of AMR 3.0. Does it include the training split of AMR 3.0? If so, there will be data leakage and the evaluation is no longer meaningful. According to the DocAMR paper, only 9 test graphs are not coming from the training split of AMR 3.0, which are too few.

**Response**: To avoid any possibility of data leakage, our DocAMR evaluation uses only the nine document-level graphs whose constituent sentence-level AMRs come entirely from the AMR 3.0 test split. These documents contain no AMRs from the AMR 3.0 training data, so the evaluation is fully held-out with respect to the supervision used during fine-tuning.
Although the number of document graphs is small, each document contains many sentence-level AMRs, all sourced from the AMR 3.0 test set. This allows us to stratify results by structural complexity (e.g., number of AMRs $\ge z$) while remaining within a clean, non-overlapping test partition. All DocAMR results reported in the paper are computed exclusively on this held-out subset.
We have clarified this in the revision to avoid any ambiguity (Appendix E.1).

This ensures that each reported value is computed over a meaningful number of examples while preserving the monotonic interpretation of the threshold.
For DocAMR, we address sparsity in an equally transparent way. As noted above, we evaluate only on the nine document-level graphs whose sentence-level AMRs come entirely from the AMR 3.0 test split. Although there are only nine documents, each contains many AMRs, producing a broad and dense distribution of document-level complexities (Figure 10b). As in AMR 3.0, all thresholds $z$ represent the set of documents with complexity $\geq z$, which provides more stable estimates within the constraints of the available test data.

summary.value:
This paper proposes a structure-aware fine-tuning approach named SAFT for the AMR-to-Text task, aiming to enhance large language models’ understanding of graph-structured data. The SAFT method first transforms the original AMR graph into a directed, edge-unlabeled semantic-preserving graph (SPG), which preserves the structural semantics of the original AMR while enabling the application of spectral methods based on the Laplacian for positional encoding. Subsequently, AMR-specific graph positional encodings are derived using the magnetic Laplacian of the SPG, capturing the topological structure and directionality of the AMR graph. Finally, these graph positional encodings are incorporated into token embeddings, enabling relational inductive bias without modifying the model architecture.

Experimental results on the AMR 3.0 dataset demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms direct fine-tuning of large models using LoRA, particularly on graph structures with greater depth.

strengths.value: The paper proposes a novel graph structure encoding method that effectively encodes the structural information of AMR graphs. Furthermore, this method appears to be compatible with any Decoder-only LLM and holds potential for adaptation to other graph structures.

weaknesses.value:
1.  **Lack of Important Baselines:** Prompt-based methods are also model-agnostic and, crucially, do not require additional training, potentially offering stronger generalization. The authors do not compare their method against such approaches in the main text. Although a comparison with a GPT-4o-mini zero-shot method is included in Appendix C.4, this is insufficient because: 

(a) The comparison is unfair: a comparison with *few-shot* methods is more appropriate, given that the proposed SAFT involves additional training on the AMR 3.0 dataset. 

(b) Few-shot prompt-based experiments should be added for *all* models used in Table 1 (LLaMA 3.2 1B, 3B, Qwen2.5 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, and Gemma 2B) to justify the necessity of fine-tuning, especially since fine-tuning consumes significant resources and often severely degrades the model's general capabilities.

2.  **Unfair Experimental Comparisons:**

(a) The model sizes of the baselines in the upper part of Table 1 are not comparable to those in the lower part. For instance, the largest model used in StructAdapt (T5-Large) has about 0.77B (770M) parameters, while the LLMs for which SAFT outperforms StructAdapt all have 1.5B parameters or more (at least 1.94x larger than T5-Large).


 (b) When the parameter size of SAFT is comparable to StructAdapt, its performance is actually worse. Specifically, in Table 1, the BLEU and CHRF++ scores for Qwen2.5 0.5B, LLaMA 3.2 1B, and StructAdapt (0.77B) are 42.9 < 47.8 < 48.0 and 69.3 < 71.9 < 73.2, respectively.


3.  **Lack of Generalization Experiments:** Although the authors state that the proposed method is applicable to other tasks involving graph-structured inputs (Lines 78-79), they provide no experiments to substantiate this claim. Furthermore, given that experiments were conducted solely on the AMR 3.0 dataset, it is necessary to supplement the paper with experiments on other datasets involving graph-structured inputs to properly evaluate the method's generalization capability.

Thank you for the thoughtful review. We appreciate your comments on the novelty and potential of our approach to enhance LLM's understanding of graph-structured data. We address your points below:

### Comparison with few-shot methods (W1.a)
**Comment**: a comparison with few-shot methods is more appropriate, given that the proposed SAFT involves additional training on the AMR 3.0 dataset.

**Response**: We go beyond zero-shot evaluation by including **few-shot prompting results on both GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o**, a significantly larger and instruction-tuned model. We integrated these results into **Section 4.5 and Table 2** in the revised version. Even with carefully designed few-shot examples, the improvements over zero-shot prompting are small, and both models remain far below the performance of fine-tuned models that are orders of magnitude smaller. We report the results here for completeness:

| Model          | Setting   | BLEU | METEOR | ChrF  | BERTScore |
|----------------|-----------|------|--------|-------|-----------|
| GPT‑4o-mini    | zero‑shot | 16.3 | 38.4   | 44.8  | 74.8      |
| GPT‑4o-mini    | few‑shot  | 17.0 | 39.9   | 45.2  | 75.7      |
| GPT‑4o         | zero‑shot | 28.0 | 52.1   | 59.8  | 81.1      |
| GPT‑4o         | few‑shot  | 29.6 | 52.4   | 60.1  | 81.8      |
| Qwen 2.5 (3B)  | FT        | 51.6 | 59.4   | 72.1  | 82.9      |
| Qwen 2.5 (3B)  | SAFT      | **51.9** | **60.1** | **74.8** | **83.7** |

We believe that the key factor behind this difference in performance stems from the level of supervision. A small set of in-context examples does not provide sufficient signals to learn the mappings involved in AMR-to-text generation in a zero-shot or few-shot setting. Fine-tuning, on the other hand, can benefit from supervision over the entire training set and can also adjust parameters to align with it, resulting in higher performance.

SAFT adds another source of signal through graph-aware positional encodings. In the results we report, this provides steady improvements over standard fine-tuning across different model families and sizes. In summary, the experiments suggest that **injecting explicit structural information during fine-tuning offers benefits that few-shot prompting on much larger models did not match**.

**Comment**: Few-shot prompt-based experiments should be added for all models used in Table 1 (LLaMA 3.2 1B, 3B, Qwen2.5 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, and Gemma 2B) to justify the necessity of fine-tuning, especially since fine-tuning consumes significant resources and often severely degrades the model's general capabilities.

**Response**: We appreciate the reviewer's suggestion and understand the motivation for exploring few-shot performance on the smaller models in Table 1. This suggests that, for AMR-to-text, the limitation does not appear to be solely due to model scale, but rather to the lack of task-specific supervision and structural information in the prompting setup (as discussed above).
Given this pattern, we expect few-shot prompting on smaller, non-instruction-tuned models will be limited in absolute performance. However, we are running these experiments for completeness, and initial experiments on Qwen 0.5B (few-shot) support our claims

| Model            | Setting   | BLEU | METEOR | ChrF  | BERTScore |
|------------------|-----------|------|--------|-------|-----------|

### Experimental comparison (W2.a and W2.b)
**Comment(s)**: (a) The model sizes of the baselines in the upper part of Table 1 are not comparable to those in the lower part. (b) When the parameter size of SAFT is comparable to StructAdapt, its performance is actually worse. Specifically, in Table 1, the BLEU and ChrF scores for Qwen2.5 0.5B, LLaMA 3.2 1B, and StructAdapt (0.77B) are 42.9 < 47.8 < 48.0 and 69.3 < 71.9 < 73.2, respectively.

**Response**: Table 1 mixes prior encoder–decoder AMR-to-text baselines with our experiments on decoder-only LLMs. This is deliberate. The goal is not to present a size-matched leaderboard, but to clarify what decoder-only models can and cannot do in this setting.

First, to our knowledge, this is the first work that systematically studies decoder-only LLMs for AMR-to-text generation. We show that, after fine-tuning, these models become competitive with established AMR-specific systems in their original configurations, despite not being designed for graph-to-text translation.

Second, our comparison is primarily within the decoder-only family. On the same backbones and with identical supervision, SAFT improves over standard fine-tuning across model families and scales. This isolates the contribution of structural encoding, independently of architecture or model size.

Third, we agree that at comparable parameter scales, encoder–decoder models have inherent advantages for structured generation tasks, because they process the graph through a dedicated encoder pathway. This is also supported by StructAdapt's own ablations (Table 5 in their paper): when they remove the encoder-side graph adapters and keep only decoder-side adapters, performance drops sharply to 11.6 BLEU at a similar parameter count. This highlights that directly removing the encoder from such systems results in a fundamentally weaker model, rather than a fair decoder-only variant.

In this context, it is not surprising that StructAdapt outperforms our smallest decoder-only SAFT models. Those models are included to analyze how SAFT behaves across different scales of decoder-only models, not to claim architectural superiority. Our state-of-the-art claim refers specifically to the strongest decoder-only SAFT configuration.

We thank you for raising this point, and have revisited our position in Section 4.2.

However, the **goal of this work is to study structure-aware fine-tuning specifically in the context of AMR-to-text generation**, which is the focus of the title, abstract, and experiments
SAFT is conceptually applicable to other settings that involve graph-structured inputs, but **we do not present empirical results outside AMR** in this submission. summary.value: This paper presents a method for graph structural information and directionality encoding into an embedding space, i.e., graph structure-aware positional embeddings. The authors use the graph adjacency matrix and the magnetic Laplacian operator to derive the embeddings (further combined with token embeddings). A transformation of the original graph is carried out, to encode edge labels; this involves representing edge labels as nodes. While the approach is presented for AMR-to-text generation, it would be applicable to other concrete graphs (e.g., scene graphs). As for the integration of input graphs with LLMs, input graphs are linearized and tokenized, graph positional embeddings  (i.e., a learnt MLP combines nodes positions and tokens and maps to the LLM embedding size) are combined with the standard LLM's sequence embeddings.

Thank you for the constructive review and for recognizing the usefulness of our contribution in improving LLM tasks that require long context processing. We address your concerns below.

### Results on large-scale LLMs (W1)
**Comment**: It is not clear how would these results generalize to larger scale LLMs.

**Response**: We address the reviewer's concern in four steps.
1. First, we test whether large, general-purpose LLMs can solve AMR-to-text without fine-tuning. In the updated Table 2, we report zero-shot and few-shot results for GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o. Despite their scale, both models perform substantially worse than a 3B open-source model after being fine-tuned specifically for AMR. This suggests that, under our prompting setup, scale and general pretraining alone do not suffice to solve AMR-to-text reliably under our prompting setup.
2. Second, we examine whether structure-aware fine-tuning brings additional benefits beyond standard fine-tuning. As shown in Table 1 and in the newly added Appendix C.3 (bootstrap paired significance test) and Figure 9, SAFT typically improves over FT, with gains ranging from marginal to substantial, depending on the model and metric.
3. Third, we study where these gains come from. In Figures 2 and 3, we stratify results by structural complexity. We observe that the advantage of SAFT over FT grows as graphs become deeper and more structurally complex. When AMRs are simple, FT is often sufficient. As the structure becomes more challenging, explicit structural encoding provides increasingly beneficial effects.
4. Fourth, we analyze whether these gains diminish as models become larger. The results in Appendix C.2 (and Figure 8) show no monotonic relationship between model size and the improvement brought by SAFT. Some mid-sized models benefit most in BLEU, while larger models show stronger improvements in ChrF. This cross-family and cross-metric variability indicates that model size alone might not be a reliable predictor of how much structure-aware fine-tuning helps.

Overall, the experiments show that fine-tuning remains crucial even for very large LLMs, that structure-aware fine-tuning typically improves over conventional fine-tuning, with gains ranging from marginal to substantial, and that its benefits are driven more by structural complexity than by model scale.

### Embeddings dynamics (W3.2)
**Comment:** It would be useful to have the intuition of the dynamics of the LLM learning representations via embeddings.

**Response**: Thank you for this insightful comment. We have added an embedding dynamics analysis in **Section 4.6 (Figure 4)**, which shows that the proposed AmrPEs are largely orthogonal to the semantic embedding space, thereby expanding the representational subspace rather than overwriting it. In particular, we show that:
1. AmrPEs have a similar order of magnitude to X, ensuring that they are not obscured by X nor do they obscure X during training. 
2. The directions of our AmrPEs (structural-level semantics) are approximately orthogonal to the directions of X (textual-level semantics), demonstrating that AmrPEs add structure-level information in different directions than the textual-level semantics. 
3. When projected into the 2D PCA of X, AmrPEs express the most variance across one main direction (PC2), while the remaining variance is spread across a few more directions.
4. As a consequence of point (3), AmrPEs introduce a coherent and consistent directional shift along a few dimensions in the latent space, effectively "moving" textual representation to a different subspace;
5. The combined representations (H = X + AmrPE) span a higher-level dimensional space than X, indicating that structural information expands representational capacity, rather than collapsing it.

We hope this analysis answers your concern, and we are open to further suggestions or interpretations of our results.

### Generated outputs (Q3.1)
**Comment**: It would be illustrative to add example outputs, generated texts, by the different models.

**Response**: We now include representative outputs from both the fine-tuned baseline (FT) and our SAFT model on LLaMA 3B in **Appendix G**. These examples are selected in a principled manner using smoothed sentence-level BLEU distributions and relative performance percentiles to avoid cherry-picking. For each category (cases where SAFT is substantially better, where FT is better, where both models perform well, and where both perform poorly), we present five instances along with their reference sentences. We also provide character-level difference highlighting, allowing readers to see precisely where each model diverges from the gold text. This should provide a clearer and more grounded picture of the qualitative behavior of both models.

### Additional evaluations (Q3.2)
**Comment**: Even a human eval (or LLM-as-Judge assessing real textual differences) would strengthen the presented approach and results.

**Response**: We already include **BERTScore** [3], widely regarded as a form of *LLM-as-Judge* evaluation, in our evaluation metrics (Tables 2, 7, and 8). BERTScore leverages contextual embeddings from pretrained language models to assess semantic similarity between generated and reference texts, capturing meaning-level differences beyond surface form. **SAFT improves over FT on BERTScore** across the reported settings. In particular, as highlighted in Table 8, BERTScore gains over FT increase at increasing graph depth (complexity), suggesting that the generated texts are judged as more semantically faithful on these more complex examples. We plan to conduct the remaining evaluations and include the results in the revised paper.

### Adjacency matrix symmetrization (Q2)
**Comment**: It would be useful to motivate why it is needed to symmetrize the adjacency matrix.

**Response**: While the symmetrization of the adjacency matrix is not *always* necessary (e.g., for direction-aware GNNs), it is required in our case because we compute graph positional embeddings from the eigen decomposition (EVD) of a Laplacian matrix. When taking this spectral approach, one generally has two options: (1) symmetrize the adjacency matrix to obtain a symmetric Laplacian, which enables EVD but discards directional information; or (2) use alternative formulations such as the magnetic Laplacian, which preserves directionality by encoding it in a complex-valued phase shift, as shown in Eq. (1). Our method adopts the latter, allowing us to retain structural asymmetry while still benefiting from the spectral properties required to compute positional embeddings. We have inserted a clarifying sentence in the main text.

### Comparison to previous work (W3.1)
**Comment**: While the authors include a structure-aware fine-tuning, previous work (StructAdapt), this seems quite an old model. It would be better to report results on a re-implantation of this in the same target LLMs to better compare performance. 

**Response**: Thank you for the suggestion. While we agree that a direct comparison would be valuable in principle, StructAdapt is fundamentally designed for encoder–decoder architectures (e.g., T5), where structural information is integrated through a dedicated graph encoder whose outputs are consumed by the decoder. In contrast, our work focuses on decoder-only LLMs, which lack such an encoder pathway. Re-implementing StructAdapt in this setting would therefore require a significant redesign of its core mechanism, rather than a faithful port.

This is also supported by StructAdapt's own ablations (Table 5 in their paper): removing the encoder-side structural components (while keeping parameter count constant) causes a sharp performance drop, indicating that their method critically relies on the encoder–decoder separation. A decoder-only adaptation would not yield a controlled baseline comparison.

We therefore include StructAdapt and other encoder–decoder systems for contextualization within the AMR-to-text literature, while focusing our controlled comparisons on decoder-only models. Within this setting, we show that standard fine-tuning already makes decoder-only LLMs competitive with these earlier systems, and that SAFT further strengthens them in most settings across the tested families and scales.

### Related work on semantic transformation (W2)
**Comment**: The authors miss some important related work on graph encoding, which deals in particular with the issue of encoding edge labels and applies semantic preserving transformation/reification of edges as nodes. These should added into the related work discussion [1, 2].

**Response**: Thank you for pointing out these works (Marcheggiani & Titov, 2017; Marcheggiani & Perez-Beltrachini, 2018). We have added a short clarification in Section 3.1, noting the similarity to these approaches, which are specific to SRL and RDF graphs. We also specify that, in our case, we perform AMR-specific transformations to derive magnetic-Laplacian positional encodings, which are crucial elements for our proposed structure-aware fine-tuning approach. 

### References

[1]: Encoding Sentences with Graph Convolutional Networks for Semantic Role Labeling (https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04826) 

[2]: Deep Graph Convolutional Encoders for Structured Data to Text Generation (https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.09995)

[3]: BERTScore: Evaluating Text Generation with BERT (https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09675)

We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. Their comments helped us refine the presentation and strengthen the empirical analysis.  All changes are highlighted in the revised manuscript to make the updates easy to track.

Below, we summarize the core contributions of the paper, strengths highlighted by the reviewers, and key additions, extensions or clarifications made in response to their comments.

### Core contributions

- We introduce **SAFT**, a general framework for **structure-aware fine-tuning** of decoder-only LLMs. SAFT injects graph topology into the model's latent space using **graph positional embeddings** derived from the **Magnetic Laplacian**.
- We instantiate SAFT on **AMR-to-text generation**, a structure-to-text task that challenges large language models even under prompting. We show that SAFT consistently improves over standard fine-tuning across **multiple model families and sizes**.
- SAFT is **architecture-agnostic**, adds **minimal parameter overhead**, and works with off-the-shelf decoder-only LLMs without modifying any model's components.

### Strengths highlighted by reviewers

Reviewers noted several strengths:

- The **importance of the problem**, particularly as modern decoder-only LLMs struggle with structured inputs (e.g., AMR graphs) that are not naturally accommodated by decoder-only architectures (as opposed to encoder-decoder architectures).
- The **clarity of presentation**, extensive appendices, and accessibility to non-experts.
- The **novelty and generality** of the approach, including its potential for broader application.
- The **rigorous empirical evaluation**, including:
  - a quantitative analysis on both **AMR 3.0** and **DocAMR**;
  - a **complexity-stratified analysis**, showing the benefits of using SAFT grow with graph depth or complexity;
  - a comparisons to **large proprietary LLMs**, highlighting the strength of smaller fine-tuned models.

### Additions and revisions

In response to reviewer feedback, we introduced the following:

- **Few-shot evaluation on GPT-4o** (Sec. 4.5): We extend our evaluation to include **few-shot GPT‑4o and GPT‑4o-mini**, showing that **even large, instruction-tuned models underperform** compared to smaller SAFT-tuned models on AMR.

- **Geometric embedding analysis** (Sec. 4.6): We show that SAFT injects structural signals along **orthogonal directions** in embedding space, suggesting minimal interference with base semantics.

- **Scaling trends** (App. C.2): We analyze SAFT across model sizes (up to 3B) and find **no evidence that benefits decline with scale**. Gains remain robust, countering the view that scale alone eliminates the need for structural encoding.

- **Bootstrap significance testing** (App. C.3): We add **paired bootstrap tests**, confirming the statistical reliability of SAFT's improvements over FT across metrics and model families.

- **Efficiency clarification** (App. C.5): We make explicit that SAFT introduces **negligible overhead**: a 2-layer MLP and a one-time Laplacian EVD computation. No architectural changes or inference-time costs are incurred.

- **Clarified scope and generality** (Sec. 1, App. C.6): We clarify that while SAFT is **conceptually general**, this paper focuses specifically on **AMR-to-text**, selected for its structural richness and evaluation maturity.

- **Qualitative output comparisons** (App. G): We include representative generations from SAFT and FT, illustrating output differences and error patterns.

We hope these clarifications and additions help support a positive recommendation.

summary.value:
This paper proposes a method to encode structural information with graph-sensitive positional encodings derived from the magnetic Laplacian. Reviewers find this an important problem and recognize the novelty of the approach. While the reviewers raise a number of concerns and questions, the common ones include the lack of application of the proposed method to larger LLM models and missing experiments on other graph domains. Some reviewers also request a deeper exploration of the dynamics of LLMs in learning representations via embeddings or via explicit structural information. Additionally, several technical points were pointed out for further clarification.

In the rebuttal, the authors provided detailed responses that largely address many presentation and clarity issues. However, some major common concerns are not fully addressed. For example, regarding generalization to larger-scale LLMs, the authors did not provide new experiments applying the proposed method to larger models, such as 7B or 70B parameter LLMs, among others.

reviewer_concerns.value:
I believe the detailed responses address many of the concerns and questions raised by the reviewers. However, several major issues remain outstanding.

For Reviewer j3pi, it is suggested that the proposed method be applied to larger-scale LLMs (e.g., 7B or 70B parameters) to demonstrate its generalizability. however, the authors fail to provide such experiments. This concern is also raised by Reviewer XhwZ.
For Reviewer reLC, the authors are asked to provide generalization experiments on other domains, as the paper claims that the proposed method is applicable to other tasks involving graph-structured inputs. In the rebuttal, instead of adding one or more such scenarios, the authors tone down this claim and narrow the scope to AMR, focusing solely on that setting.
Similarly, Reviewer XhwZ raises the same concerns regarding missing experiments on other domains and the lack of evaluations on larger-scale LLMs. 
Reviewer 8wDp also questions the absence of experiments on other commonly used structure-to-text datasets. In response, the authors argue for focusing exclusively on AMR.

reviewer_scores.value: Reviewers XhwZ and 8wDp initially gave positive ratings, and I believe they are likely to maintain their original scores. For Reviewer j3pi, the major concern is not fully addressed, so I also expect this reviewer’s score to remain unchanged. Reviewer reLC initially gave a score of 2. Although several concerns and questions were largely resolved in the rebuttal, such as adding few-shot prompt-based experiments across models and addressing unfair experimental comparisons, I think the score is still likely to remain negative, as the key concern regarding the lack of generalization experiments persists.
